sections.p11.s0: The concepts behind every concurrency choice. Do items 0 to 4 as one asyncio block, then 5 and 6 on threads and processes, then races, timeouts and profiling. Write a short script for every item and keep them; the benchmark exercise reuses most of them.
sections.p11.s1: A crawler that exercises everything from the Learn section. Start with the queue and worker pool against a local test server, then add rate limiting, retries, normalisation, caching and persistence in order. Leave logs, metrics and shutdown for last, and test each feature before moving on.
sections.p11.s2: The measured comparison that justifies your concurrency choice. Build one harness first, run the I/O-bound workload three ways, then the CPU-bound one, and write up the numbers. Plan about a third of the time for the harness, a third for runs, a third for the write-up.

p11.s0.0.how: Read the Real Python concurrency article, then write two functions: one that sleeps 1 second (I/O-like) and one that sums squares to 10 million (CPU-bound). Run four of each with threads and with processes and time every run.

where.name: Real Python: Speed up your program with concurrency

p11.s0.0.done: You can explain, using your own timings, why threads speed up the sleeps but not the sums on the default build.

p11.s0.1.how: Write three coroutines that print, await asyncio.sleep, and print again, and run them with asyncio.run. Then replace one sleep with time.sleep and observe that it blocks all three. Turn on debug mode to see the slow-callback warning.
p11.s0.1.done: You can say what the event loop does at each await, and why a blocking call stalls every coroutine.

p11.s0.2.how: Fetch ten URLs from a local server three ways: asyncio.create_task plus awaits, asyncio.gather, and asyncio.TaskGroup. Make one fetch raise and compare what happens to the others in each version.
p11.s0.2.done: You can say what happens to sibling tasks when one fails under gather and under TaskGroup.

p11.s0.3.how: Write a task that holds a resource (an open file or a client) and cancel it with task.cancel(). Release the resource in try/finally or async with, and confirm CancelledError is re-raised, not swallowed.
p11.s0.3.done: Cancelling the task always closes the resource, and a test shows the task ends in the cancelled state.

p11.s0.4.how: Limit 100 fetches to 10 at once with asyncio.Semaphore, then rebuild the same thing as a producer, an asyncio.Queue(maxsize=20), and 10 workers. Print the number in flight each second to confirm the cap.
p11.s0.4.done: The in-flight count never exceeds 10, and you can say when a queue fits better than a semaphore.

p11.s0.5.how: Run 50 blocking HTTP requests through a ThreadPoolExecutor and time it against a plain loop. Then run a pure-Python CPU loop on four threads. Read the free-threading HOWTO and, if you can install a 3.13t or later build, repeat the CPU run on it.
p11.s0.5.done: You can say which operations release the GIL, and show that threads speed up I/O but not pure-Python CPU work on the default build.

p11.s0.6.how: Run a CPU-bound function over 8 inputs with ProcessPoolExecutor. Then pass a large list as an argument and time the pickling overhead. Compare with a NumPy version, which releases the GIL inside its native code.
p11.s0.6.done: You have timings showing the process speed-up and the point where pickling cost cancels it out.

p11.s0.7.how: Write a counter incremented by 8 threads with no lock and show a wrong total (add a time.sleep(0) between read and write if needed). Fix it with threading.Lock. Then create a deadlock with two locks taken in opposite orders, and fix it with a fixed lock order.
p11.s0.7.done: You can reproduce the race and the deadlock on demand and explain the fix for each.

p11.s0.8.how: Set explicit timeouts on every layer of one request path: httpx.Timeout for connect and read, asyncio.timeout around the whole operation, and a timeout on any queue get. Point it at a local server that never responds.
p11.s0.8.done: Against a server that hangs, your program fails with a timeout error within the limit you set.

p11.s0.9.how: Profile one of your scripts with python -m cProfile -s cumtime, and track memory with tracemalloc snapshots. Benchmark a function with timeit, repeating runs and reporting the median, after a warm-up, with other programs closed.
p11.s0.9.done: You can name the top three functions by cumulative time and the line that allocates the most memory.

p11.s1.0.how: Start with an asyncio.Queue of seed URLs, N worker tasks sharing one httpx.AsyncClient, and a local test site of a few hundred linked pages. Workers parse links and enqueue new ones; stop when the queue is empty and all workers are idle.
p11.s1.0.done: The crawler visits every page of the test site and exits by itself with no hanging tasks.

p11.s1.1.how: Keep a dictionary of per-host limiters (a semaphore plus a minimum delay, or a token bucket) keyed by urlparse(url).netloc. Have each worker acquire the host's limiter before fetching.
p11.s1.1.done: Request timestamps in your log show no host receives more than your configured rate.

p11.s1.2.how: Classify failures: timeouts, connection errors and 5xx are retried with backoff up to a limit; 4xx and exhausted retries go to a dead-letter table with the URL, status and last error. Test with a local server that returns each case.
p11.s1.2.done: Every URL ends either fetched or in the dead-letter table, and a 404 is never retried.

p11.s1.3.how: Write a normalise(url) function: lower-case scheme and host, drop default ports and fragments, resolve relative links with urljoin, and sort query parameters. Store seen URLs in a set and unit-test ten tricky cases.
p11.s1.3.done: Your tests show URLs that differ only in case, fragment or parameter order map to one key, and no page is fetched twice.

p11.s1.4.how: Cache responses on disk or in SQLite keyed by normalised URL, storing body, ETag and Last-Modified. On a repeat crawl send If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since and treat a 304 as a cache hit.
p11.s1.4.done: A second crawl of the unchanged test site makes mostly 304 or no requests, and your metrics show the hit rate.

p11.s1.5.how: Have workers put results on a queue, and let one writer task collect them into batches of 100 or every 2 seconds and insert them with executemany in one transaction. Compare total time against one insert per page.
p11.s1.5.done: Batched writes are measurably faster than single inserts, and no result is lost when the crawl ends mid-batch.

p11.s1.6.how: Log one JSON object per event with URL, status, duration and worker id. Keep counters for pages fetched, errors, queue size and in-flight requests, and print them every few seconds or expose them with prometheus_client.
p11.s1.6.done: While the crawl runs you can read pages per second and error count live, and filter the log by URL.

p11.s1.7.how: Catch Ctrl+C: asyncio.run turns SIGINT into cancellation of the main task (use loop.add_signal_handler on Unix if you want your own handler). Stop taking new URLs, let in-flight fetches finish with a time limit, flush the final batch, then exit.
p11.s1.7.done: Pressing Ctrl+C mid-crawl exits within your time limit, and every page reported fetched is in the database.

p11.s2.0.how: Write one harness that takes a workload function and a runner (loop, ThreadPoolExecutor, asyncio.gather with a semaphore). Use the same URL list against a local server with fixed latency so network noise does not dominate.
p11.s2.0.done: All three runners complete the same workload and produce the same set of results.

p11.s2.1.how: Record per-request durations with time.perf_counter and compute p50 and p95 with statistics.quantiles. Sample CPU and memory with psutil. Inject failures at a set rate on the server and record how each runner copes.
p11.s2.1.done: You have a table with throughput, p50, p95, peak CPU, peak memory and error handling for each runner, averaged over at least three runs.

p11.s2.2.how: Swap in a CPU-bound workload such as hashing or prime counting and run it sequentially, with threads, and with ProcessPoolExecutor. Vary worker count from 1 to your core count and record the speed-up.
p11.s2.2.done: Your numbers show processes scaling with cores while threads stay near sequential speed on the default build.

p11.s2.3.how: Write one page: the workloads, the machine and Python version, the method, a results table, and a recommendation for which model to use for each workload type. State the limits of your test.

where.name: Real Python: Speed up your program with concurrency

p11.s2.3.done: Someone else could rerun your benchmark from the page and reach the same recommendation.
